title: Myself
description: Say what you do to yourself.

explanation.summary: A reflexive verb is an action you do to yourself. The pronoun it takes is called reflexive, and it comes from the person doing the action. Not all of them are about your body: acordarse, to remember, is reflexive too.

sections.heading: The forms
sections.body: The reflexive pronouns are me, te, se, nos, os, se. They are the same for every reflexive verb: me ducho, te duchas, se ducha, nos duchamos, os ducháis, se duchan. The verbs themselves keep their normal ending, with the addition of -se: duchar becomes ducharse, and in the infinitive the se is attached: ducharse.

examples.en: Do you go to bed late?

sections.heading: Not only about the body
sections.body: Several verbs take a reflexive pronoun for a meaning that is not about the body. Acordarse is to remember, beware is to be careful, and legalization is to get legalised. And the pronoun can be dropped when it is obvious:voy a duchar, I am going to shower.

examples.es: Hay que tener cuidado con el agua.
examples.en: You have to be careful with the water.

sections.heading: When the pronoun changes the meaning
sections.body: With a reflexive pronoun the action is done to yourself, and without it it is done to someone else. Levantar is to lift: levanto la caja, I lift the box. Levantarse is to get up: me levanto, I get up. And in the negative, the reflexive pronoun is what makes it reflexive: no me levanto, I do not get up.

examples.en: I am not getting up today.

exercises.prompt: Pair each word with its translation.
exercises.note: A reflexive verb takes a reflexive pronoun: me ducho, se lava. The pronoun usually comes first.

exercises.prompt: Pick the Spanish word for “to shower”.
exercises.note: A reflexive verb: me ducho, te duchas, se ducha.
The reflexive pronoun comes before the verb.
